questions.stem: People recalled lists of letters. Which result is found with lists of similar-sounding items, and what does it show about the code used in short-term memory?
options: Lists of similar-sounding items were recalled worse than lists of different-sounding items, showing a speech-based code.
Lists of similar-looking items were recalled worse than lists of different-looking items, showing a purely visual code.
Lists of similar-sounding items were recalled better than lists of different-sounding items, showing sound helps recall.
Lists of similar-sounding items and different-sounding items were recalled equally well, showing no code is used.
questions.why: Similar-sounding items are recalled worse, which is the phonological (acoustic) similarity effect. This points to a speech-based code. A visual code would predict look-alike confusions, not sound-alike ones, and the similarity cost is a cost, not a benefit or a null result.

questions.stem: In an articulatory suppression condition, participants keep their speech machinery busy while they study lists. What was this manipulation designed to test?
options: Whether blocking the conversion of visual input into a speech code would remove the similar-sounding cost.
Whether people can remember more items when they speak aloud than when they stay silent.
Whether visually similar letters are confused more often than acoustically similar letters.
Whether the sensory store lasts longer when the articulatory machinery is occupied.
questions.why: Articulatory suppression keeps the articulatory control process busy so recoding into speech cannot happen. If the similarity effect depends on that recoding, it should vanish. The other options describe different questions (speaking aloud benefits, visual confusions, sensory store duration) that the manipulation was not built to address.

questions.stem: A student silently looks at the letters B, D, G, P, T, V and then writes them from memory, making several errors. Which kind of error would the phonological similarity effect lead you to expect?
options: Swapping letters that sound alike, such as writing B in place of D.
Swapping letters that look alike, such as writing E in place of F.
Forgetting the first letters of the list but remembering the final ones accurately.
Remembering the letters perfectly because silent viewing avoids any speech code.
questions.why: These letters sound alike, and people recode silent visual input into a speech form, so sound-alike items get confused. Look-alike confusions would indicate a visual code, and silent viewing does not prevent recoding.

questions.stem: Roodenrys et al. (2002) compared recall of words from large and small neighborhoods in a short-term memory task. What did Roodenrys et al. (2002) find?
options: People recalled more large-neighborhood words than small-neighborhood words.
People recalled more small-neighborhood words than large-neighborhood words.
People recalled large- and small-neighborhood words equally well.
People recalled large-neighborhood words better only when the words sounded alike.
questions.why: Roodenrys et al. (2002) found better recall for large-neighborhood words, showing that long-term memory factors influence short-term memory. Better recall for small neighborhoods, equal recall, or a sound-similarity condition do not match their result.

questions.stem: In memory research, a word's neighborhood can be defined in two ways. Which pair of definitions is correct?
options: The words that differ from it by one letter (orthographic) or by one sound (phonological).
The words that appear near it on a list (orthographic) or that rhyme with it (phonological).
The words with the same meaning (orthographic) or the same first sound (phonological).
The words that differ from it by one syllable (orthographic) or by one meaning (phonological).
questions.why: A neighborhood is the set of words differing by one letter or one sound. List position, rhyme alone, shared meaning, and syllable-level differences are not how neighborhood is defined.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to use memory span as a pure measure of how much a person's short-term memory can hold. According to the neighborhood size effect, what problem does this plan face?
options: Span depends partly on long-term memory factors such as word neighborhood, so it is not a pure capacity measure.
Span depends only on how fast people can speak, so it measures speech rate instead of capacity.
Span is the same for every word list, so it cannot reveal individual differences.
Span is determined entirely by the sensory store, so it measures perception rather than short-term memory.
questions.why: Because large-neighborhood words are recalled better, long-term memory influences span, so span is not purely short-term capacity. Speech rate only, identical spans, and sensory-store determination are not implied by the effect.

questions.stem: In the Brown-Peterson task, counting backwards is very different from remembering letters. Which explanation of the forgetting did the researchers therefore judge unlikely?
options: Interference from other material, rather than decay.
Decay over time, rather than interference.
A failure of attention, rather than interference.
A failure of the sensory store, rather than decay.
questions.why: Counting backwards is so unlike remembering letters that interference seemed an unlikely cause, and the researchers concluded decay. The other options name explanations they did not set aside.

questions.stem: In the Brown-Peterson task, participants do a distracting task such as counting between seeing the letters and recalling them. Why does counting suit the goal of testing decay?
options: It blocks rehearsal, and because counting is so unlike remembering letters the researchers judged it an unlikely cause of interference.
It strengthens the memory trace, because counting is similar to remembering letters.
It adds new letters to memory, which creates interference between the letters.
It keeps attention on the letters, so rehearsal continues during the delay.
questions.why: The distractor stops rehearsal, and since it is unlike the letters, the researchers judged interference an unlikely cause of any forgetting, which isolates decay. Strengthening, adding letters, or encouraging rehearsal would defeat that purpose.

questions.stem: In a Brown-Peterson style study, recall gets worse the longer people are kept from rehearsing the letters. Which conclusion did Peterson and Peterson (1959) draw from this pattern?
options: Short-term memory loses information through decay when rehearsal is blocked.
Short-term memory keeps information indefinitely whether or not it is rehearsed.
Short-term memory loses information only when similar letters appear on the list.
Short-term memory is not involved in recalling letters after a delay.
questions.why: As the distraction gets longer, recall worsens, and Peterson and Peterson concluded that short-term memory loses information through decay unless it is rehearsed. This is the researchers' conclusion. Indefinite retention, similarity-only loss, and no involvement contradict the pattern.

questions.stem: What is the modality effect in memory for lists?
options: Better memory for the last one or two items when a list is heard than when it is looked at silently.
Better memory for the first one or two items when a list is looked at silently than when it is heard.
Better memory for the middle items of a list when the list is heard rather than seen.
Better memory for all items when a list is shown in the same sense as the test.
questions.why: The modality effect is an advantage for the final items of a heard list over a silently viewed one. The other options name the wrong items or the wrong direction.

questions.stem: Which explanation of the modality effect do Neath and Surprenant (2003) offer?
options: Hearing a list gives an extra type of information, how it sounds, which helps with the final items.
Hearing a list makes people rehearse it faster, which helps with the first items.
Hearing a list blocks the speech code, which helps with the middle items.
Hearing a list removes the need for any memory store, which helps with all items.
questions.why: Neath and Surprenant (2003) argued that auditory presentation provides extra sound information that helps the final items. The other explanations propose rehearsal speed, blocked speech codes, or no store, none of which they gave.

questions.stem: The modality effect strongly influenced ideas about sensory memory. How is sensory memory characterized?
options: A back-up store of raw, unanalyzed sensory input that can help recall when its information is useful.
A permanent store of facts and meanings that supports recall after long delays.
A rehearsal loop that converts visual input into a speech code.
A store of well-analyzed information that is kept only for the most important items.
questions.why: Sensory memory holds raw, unanalyzed sensory input as a back-up. A permanent knowledge store, a rehearsal loop, and a store of analyzed items describe other systems.

questions.stem: Earlier work suggested that people can report only a small part of a brief glance. What did Sperling (1960) argue about the cause of that limit?
options: The limit came from recalling what was seen, not from perceiving it.
The limit came from perceiving too little, because the glance was too short to register the items.
The limit came from the display being unreadable, so the items never reached memory.
The limit came from interference between the items during the glance itself.
questions.why: Sperling (1960) argued the limit reflected recall, since a cue right after the display allowed almost perfect report of the cued part, showing that nearly everything had been perceived. The other options place the limit in perception or the display.

questions.stem: Why did Sperling (1960) ask participants to report only a cued part of the display, rather than the whole display?
options: So the limit on how much can be recalled would not hide how much of the display was still available.
So participants could rehearse the whole display before the cue arrived.
So participants would report the entire display faster than before.
So participants would pay attention only to the part they expected to be cued.
questions.why: Reporting only a cued part avoids the recall limit, so accuracy for that part estimates what was held from the whole display. The cue was not meant to allow rehearsal, speed up full report, or direct attention beforehand.

questions.stem: In a partial report study, accuracy for the cued part is very high when the cue comes immediately but falls back to the usual low level when the cue is delayed. What does the drop show?
options: The sensory (iconic) store holds a lot of information, but only very briefly.
The sensory store holds only a few items, whatever the delay.
The sensory store lasts a long time, so delays do not matter.
The sensory store is created by the cue, so late cues cannot use it.
questions.why: High report with immediate cues shows a large store, and the fall with delay shows it lasts only briefly. A fixed small capacity, a long-lasting store, or a cue-created store do not fit.

questions.stem: What does the position error effect say about how people remember the order of items?
options: Items are usually recalled in the correct position, and the errors that occur are systematic rather than random.
Items are usually recalled in the wrong position, and the errors that occur are random.
Items are recalled in the correct position only when the list is heard.
Items are recalled in the correct position only when the list is short.
questions.why: The position error effect: order is usually right and errors are systematic. Mostly wrong, random errors, or a modality-only or length-only restriction are not what it states.

questions.stem: A student studies seven words in order and recalls them, putting several words one place away from where they belong. Which description of the student's memory fits the position error effect?
options: The student retains approximate position information for the words, so forgetting is not total loss.
The student has lost the words completely, because misplaced words show information was erased.
The student guessed the order at random, because misplaced words show no position information.
The student relied only on a visual code, because misplaced words look alike.
questions.why: Systematic near-miss errors show approximate position information is retained. Complete loss, random guessing, and a visual-code explanation do not fit.

questions.stem: Why can scoring recall only as percent correct give a misleading picture of forgetting order information?
options: It treats a nearby wrong position as total loss, hiding that people still retain approximate position information.
It treats a correct position as an error, hiding that people forget most items.
It treats random guesses as correct, hiding that people retain no position information.
It treats spoken items as written items, hiding the difference between sounds and meanings.
questions.why: A strict percent-correct score counts every misplaced item as wrong, even though errors are systematic and show retained approximate position. The other options misdescribe how the scoring works.

questions.stem: Shepard and Metzler (1971) showed people two block shapes and asked whether they were the same or mirror images. What did their findings suggest about mental images?
options: Mental images are much like real images, because rotating one takes time, as with a real object.
Mental images are very different from real images, because they can be rotated instantly.
Mental images are less reliable than descriptions, because people cannot rotate them.
Mental images are stored only as words, because people describe the shapes aloud.
questions.why: Shepard and Metzler (1971) suggested that mental rotation takes time like real rotation, so mental images are much like real images. Instant rotation, no rotation, and word-only storage contradict this.

questions.stem: In the task of Shepard and Metzler (1971), one block shape was turned relative to the other before people judged whether they were the same or mirror images. Why was one shape turned?
options: So that deciding required rotating a mental image, letting researchers see how that rotation behaves.
So that the shapes would look more different, making the judgment easier.
So that people would use words instead of images to compare the shapes.
So that people would rely on their own descriptions of their images.
questions.why: Turning one shape forces a mental rotation to compare them, revealing how mental imagery works. It does not make the task easier, encourage verbal strategies, or depend on self-description.

questions.stem: Suppose you count the windows in your home by picturing it. Which conclusion about mental images fits the finding that they behave like real images?
options: Mental images behave like real images, so tasks like this one can be done by inspecting an image.
Mental images behave nothing like real images, so this task cannot involve imagery.
Mental images can be trusted completely, because people's descriptions of them are accurate.
Mental images are only a verbal list, so counting depends on words alone.
questions.why: Mental images behave like real images, so tasks such as counting windows can be done by inspecting an image. The other options deny that or claim images are verbal or perfectly trustworthy.

questions.stem: In judging probability, what are heuristics?
options: Quick strategies that trade accuracy for speed and are usually good enough, but can produce wrong judgments.
Careful calculations that trade speed for accuracy and are never wrong.
Random guesses that ignore all information about the situation.
Emotional reactions that replace judgment of probability altogether.
questions.why: Heuristics trade accuracy for speed, are usually adequate, but can yield wrong judgments. Careful calculation, random guesses, and emotion-only reactions are not heuristics in this sense.

questions.stem: A person reads a short description of a quiet, bookish woman and says it is more likely that she is a librarian who also plays the violin than that she is a librarian. Which error is this?
options: The conjunction fallacy, thinking that A and B together are more likely than A alone.
The framing effect, giving a different answer because the options are worded differently.
The phonological similarity effect, confusing items that sound alike.
The modality effect, remembering heard items better than seen items.
questions.why: Rating a combination as more likely than one of its parts is the conjunction fallacy. The other options are different effects.

questions.stem: Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990) had people read short descriptions of a person and rate how likely the person was to have certain professions or activities. What did they find?
options: Sometimes people rated the combination of two professions or activities as more likely than one of its parts.
People always rated the combination as less likely than each of its parts.
People rated every profession or activity as equally likely.
People refused to rate a combination because it could not be judged.
questions.why: Shafir, Smith, and Osherson (1990) found that in some cases the combination was rated more likely than a part, the conjunction fallacy. Always lower ratings, equal ratings, or refusal are not their finding.

questions.stem: In the Wason Selection Task with the rule 'If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other side,' which cards do people typically choose?
options: D and 3, where the 3 can only confirm the rule and the 7, which could falsify it, is missed.
D and 7, the cards that could show the rule is broken.
Only the 7, since it is the only card that matters.
All four cards, since any of them could break the rule.
questions.why: People typically pick D and 3, but the back of the 3 can only confirm the rule, while the 7 could falsify it. D and 7 is the correct pair, not the typical choice.

questions.stem: Wason and Shapiro (1971) compared abstract rules with thematic rules. What did they find about when people can test a rule well?
options: People can test a rule when they have relevant experience, as with a familiar thematic rule.
People can test a rule only when it is abstract and free of everyday content.
People can test a rule equally well regardless of its content or their experience.
People can test a rule only when they are told which cards to turn over.
questions.why: Wason and Shapiro (1971) found that familiar thematic rules are easier because experience helps. Abstract-only, content-independent, and instruction-dependent claims do not fit.

questions.stem: Two groups test rules with the same logic. One group tests 'If you borrow my car, you must fill up the gas tank,' and the other tests 'If a card has a D on one side, it has a 3 on the other side.' Which group should do better, and why?
options: The car group, because familiar content draws on relevant experience.
The card group, because abstract content invites falsification.
Neither group, because the logic is identical so performance must match.
The card group, because familiar content makes people look only for confirmation.
questions.why: Thematic rules are much easier than abstract rules because people can use relevant experience. Identical logic does not guarantee identical performance.

questions.stem: What is a framing effect?
options: A case in which the wording or context makes a big difference even when the situations are otherwise equivalent.
A case in which people choose the option with the best outcome regardless of how it is worded.
A case in which people forget a choice because it was worded in an unfamiliar way.
A case in which people change their choice only because the options themselves differ.
questions.why: In a framing effect, wording or context changes choices even though the situations are otherwise equivalent. Wording-independent choice, forgetting, and changes caused by real option differences do not define it.

questions.stem: Researchers studying framing present the same choice in two different ways. Why is it important that the two versions are otherwise equivalent?
options: So any difference in choices can be attributed to the wording or context rather than to the options.
So participants will not notice that they are being tested on their decisions.
So participants will choose the better outcome in both versions.
So the outcomes can be made to differ while the wording stays the same.
questions.why: If the situations are equivalent, a difference in choice can only come from the framing. The other options misstate the purpose.

questions.stem: A company announces a plan to 'save 200 of 600 jobs' to one group and a plan that 'will lose 400 of 600 jobs' to another group, and the two groups choose differently. What does this illustrate?
options: A framing effect, because equivalent outcomes were worded differently and choices changed.
A modality effect, because one group heard the plan and the other saw it.
A conjunction fallacy, because the plans combined two outcomes.
A neighborhood size effect, because the plans used similar words.
questions.why: The two plans describe equivalent outcomes with different wording, and the choice changed: a framing effect. The other options name unrelated effects.

questions.stem: In the Monty Hall 3 Door problem, you pick one door, and Monty Hall, who always plays fair this way, opens another door to show no prize. What should you do?
options: Switch to the other closed door, because switching wins about two-thirds of the time.
Stay with your door, because staying wins about two-thirds of the time.
Choose at random, because the two remaining doors are equally likely.
Switch only if your first pick was the door on the left.
questions.why: Your first pick has a 1 in 3 chance, so the other two doors together hold 2 in 3, and the opened door shows no prize, leaving all of that on the other closed door. Staying wins about one-third and random choice about half.

questions.stem: In the Monty Hall 3 Door problem, why do many people wrongly think that staying and switching are equally good?
options: They treat the two remaining doors as equally likely, ignoring that the first pick keeps its original chance.
They believe the host moves the prize after the contestant chooses.
They believe the first pick is certain to be correct once a door is opened.
They believe the host opens doors at random, including the prize door.
questions.why: People see two closed doors and call it even, but the first pick still has only a one in three chance, so the other closed door holds the rest. The other options are not the usual mistake.

questions.stem: In research on choices between a sure outcome and a gamble, what pattern do people typically show?
options: They avoid risk with gains by taking the sure thing, and seek risk with losses by taking the gamble.
They seek risk with gains by taking the gamble, and avoid risk with losses by taking the sure thing.
They avoid risk with both gains and losses by always taking the sure thing.
They seek risk with both gains and losses by always taking the gamble.
questions.why: In prospect-theory research, people typically avoid risk with gains and seek risk with losses. The other patterns reverse or flatten it.

questions.stem: A person is offered a sure gain or a gamble that could win more but might win nothing, with the same average payoff. Based on the typical pattern, which is the person most likely to choose?
options: The sure gain, because people usually avoid risk with gains.
The gamble, because people usually seek risk with gains.
The gamble, because people usually prefer the larger possible win whatever the odds.
Either at random, because the pattern does not apply when the average payoff is equal.
questions.why: People typically take the sure thing for gains. Seeking risk is the typical pattern for losses, not gains.
